8.5 million because a woman was paralyzed on the left side?

Lawyer gets his cut because Yellow Cab wasn't going to hand over the money without a fight. And it was surely on a contingency basis as the average Jane can't cover those costs out of pocket. Now that she is paralyzed on her left side, she won't be very employable, so lifetime lost earnings. Those amounts aren't what they seem. First off, they include attorney's fees for years of trial litigation, which @ $400/hr is a lot of money. Second, the punitive portion is usually based on the amount of money the company stood to gain by doing what they supposedly should not have been doing. For example, in the famous McDonald's hot coffee case, the multimillion dollar penalty wasn't because the jury felt the lady deserved millions of dollars. It was the amount of money McDonald's made, on the day she was burned, on the coffee that they sold at a different temperature to senior citizens. The woman just happened to be lucky it was such a large amount. The intention of the penalty is not to reward the plaintiff; it's to punish the defendant enough to discourage further illicit behavior. If a company makes 30 million dollars a day breaking the law, they won't care if the penalty they need to pay to people who sue them over it is $1000. They'll just pay those people what amounts to corporate as a paltry sum, and nothing will change. If they get a penalty that hits the bottom line, they can't just pay people to go away. They have to make changes.

Yes, if there was a proper national health care system the injured party would be taken care of and would have far reduced grounds for a lawsuit. It's good economics, which is why France and the rest did it decades ago.

That wouldn't address the issue of punishing the company for wrongdoing. See this article on the $26 million verdict. The wife of the injured party was awarded $4 million. That's not for medical expenses. She wasn't even in the car. It's punitive damages that are intended to punish the company and send a message to the industry. And that's exactly what the jury did. With this penalty they sent a pretty strong message that companies must insure their drivers. Uber and Lyft give a fuck now. Before that, they didn't care that they were operating on shaky legal ground, since they were raking in the dough.

Whether you agree with the verdict or not, understand it has zero, nothing, nada, to do with the state of healthcare in the USA.
